notes.definition: Adaptations are features that enable an organism to survive in the conditions in which it normally lives. They may be structural, behavioural or functional.
explanation: Organisms have features (adaptations) that help them to survive and reproduce in the conditions where they live. Adaptations arise by natural selection over many generations: individuals with useful variations are more likely to survive and pass on their genes. AQA groups adaptations into three types: structural, behavioural and functional. In the exam you may be given information about an organism and its habitat and asked to explain how it is adapted.

Structural adaptations are features of an organism's body shape or structure. Examples include the thick fur and layer of blubber of a polar bear, which insulate it against the cold; the small ears and compact rounded body of an Arctic fox, which give a small surface area to volume ratio and reduce heat loss; the large ears of a desert fox, which increase heat loss; white fur for camouflage in snow; the spines of a cactus, which are reduced leaves that lose little water and deter animals that might eat the plant; and the long, wide-spreading or deep roots of desert plants that absorb as much water as possible.

Behavioural adaptations are the ways an organism behaves. Many desert animals are nocturnal: they shelter in burrows during the hot day and come out at night when it is cooler, so they lose less water. Some birds migrate to warmer countries in winter when food is scarce. Some mammals hibernate through cold winters. Animals such as lizards bask in the sun to warm up in the morning, and many animals huddle together to keep warm.

Functional adaptations are related to processes inside the organism, such as metabolism and reproduction. Desert animals such as camels and kangaroo rats produce very concentrated urine and little sweat, so they conserve water. Some animals lower their metabolic rate when they hibernate. Many desert plants open their stomata only at night when it is cooler, reducing water loss. Some animals time their breeding so young are born when food is plentiful.

Plants in dry places (such as cacti) show a set of adaptations: a thick waxy cuticle to reduce evaporation; spines instead of broad leaves to reduce surface area for water loss; a swollen stem to store water; fewer stomata, often sunken; and extensive roots. Plants in shady woodland often have large, broad leaves with lots of chlorophyll to absorb as much of the limited light as possible.

Some organisms live in environments that are very extreme, such as at high temperature, high pressure, or high salt concentration. These organisms are called extremophiles. Bacteria living in deep sea vents are extremophiles: they live at very high pressure and at temperatures that can be well above 100 °C in the water around the vents. Their enzymes are adapted so that they do not denature at these temperatures. Other extremophiles live in very salty lakes or in hot springs.
keyFacts: Adaptations help organisms survive in the conditions where they normally live.
Structural adaptations are physical features (for example thick fur, spines, small ears).
Behavioural adaptations are the way an organism behaves (for example being nocturnal, migrating, hibernating).
Functional adaptations involve body processes such as metabolism and reproduction (for example concentrated urine).
Animals in cold places often have a small surface area to volume ratio to reduce heat loss.
Animals in hot places often have large ears or thin bodies to increase heat loss.
Desert plants have spines, thick waxy cuticles, water-storing stems and extensive roots.
Extremophiles live in extreme conditions of high temperature, high pressure or high salt concentration.
Bacteria living in deep sea vents are extremophiles.

keyTerms.definition: A feature that enables an organism to survive in the conditions in which it normally lives.
A feature of an organism's body structure or shape, such as thick fur or spines.
The way an organism behaves that helps it survive, such as migration or being active at night.
A feature of an organism's internal processes, such as metabolism or reproduction, that helps it survive.
An organism that lives in an environment that is very extreme, such as high temperature, high pressure or high salt concentration.
The surface area of an organism divided by its volume; a smaller ratio means relatively less surface to lose heat or water from.
Colouring or pattern that helps an organism blend in with its surroundings, so it is hidden from predators or prey.
Active at night and resting during the day.

equations.name: Surface area to volume ratio
equations.formula: surface area to volume ratio = surface area ÷ volume
equations.units: no units if both are in matching units (for example cm² ÷ cm³ gives a ratio per cm)

workedExamples.title: Classifying adaptations
workedExamples.question: Classify each adaptation of a camel as structural, behavioural or functional: (a) wide feet; (b) producing very little urine; (c) resting in the shade in the hottest part of the day.
steps: Wide feet are part of the camel's body shape, which spread its weight on soft sand: structural.
Producing little, concentrated urine is a process inside the body (kidney function): functional.
Choosing to rest in shade is something the camel does: behavioural.

workedExamples.title: Comparing surface area to volume ratios
workedExamples.question: Model a small animal as a cube of side 1 cm and a larger animal as a cube of side 3 cm. Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of each, and explain which would lose heat more slowly in the Arctic.
steps: Small cube: surface area = 6 × 1 × 1 = 6 cm²; volume = 1 cm³; ratio = 6 ÷ 1 = 6.
Large cube: surface area = 6 × 3 × 3 = 54 cm²; volume = 27 cm³; ratio = 54 ÷ 27 = 2.
The larger cube has the smaller ratio: less surface per unit of volume to lose heat through.
workedExamples.answer: 6 : 1 for the small animal and 2 : 1 for the large animal; the large animal loses heat more slowly.

workedExamples.title: Explaining a desert plant's adaptations
workedExamples.question: Explain how spines and a thick waxy cuticle help a cactus survive in a desert.
steps: Spines are reduced leaves with a very small surface area, so little water evaporates from them.
Spines also protect the water-storing stem from animals.
A thick waxy cuticle is waterproof, so less water is lost by evaporation from the stem surface.
workedExamples.answer: Both features reduce water loss, which is vital where water is scarce; spines also deter animals from eating the cactus.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think organisms develop adaptations during their lifetime because they need them.
misconceptions.right: In fact adaptations arise by natural selection over many generations: individuals that already have useful variations survive and breed more.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often say hibernation or migration is a functional adaptation.
misconceptions.right: In fact migration and the decision to hibernate are behaviours, so they are behavioural adaptations. The lowered metabolic rate during hibernation is functional.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a cactus has spines only for protection.
misconceptions.right: In fact spines are reduced leaves; their small surface area greatly reduces water loss, as well as deterring animals.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think extremophiles are only bacteria in hot water.
misconceptions.right: In fact extremophiles include organisms living at high pressure or high salt concentration too; deep sea vent bacteria are just one example.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a large animal has a large surface area to volume ratio.
misconceptions.right: In fact larger, more compact animals have a smaller surface area to volume ratio, which helps them keep heat in cold climates.

realWorld: Enzymes from extremophile bacteria in hot springs (such as Taq polymerase) are used in laboratory DNA copying because they do not denature at high temperatures.
Plant breeders select crops with adaptations such as deep roots and waxy leaves to grow in areas affected by drought.
Engineers have copied the structure of polar bear fur and penguin feathers to design better insulating materials.
examTips: For 'explain how the organism is adapted' questions, give the feature and then its benefit: 'thick blubber, which insulates the body and reduces heat loss'. A feature alone usually scores only half.
Use the information given in the question: link each adaptation to a condition described (cold, dry, low light, predators).
Be ready to classify adaptations: structural (body), behavioural (actions), functional (processes inside the body).
When surface area to volume ratio is involved, state whether it is larger or smaller and what that means for heat or water loss.
summary: Adaptations enable organisms to survive in their normal conditions.
Structural: body features. Behavioural: actions. Functional: internal processes such as metabolism and reproduction.
Cold climate animals reduce heat loss: thick fur, blubber, small ears, small SA:V.
Hot, dry climate organisms reduce water loss and lose heat: nocturnal habits, concentrated urine, large ears, spines, waxy cuticles.
Extremophiles live at high temperature, pressure or salt concentration.
Bacteria in deep sea vents are extremophiles.

flashcards.back: A feature that enables an organism to survive in the conditions in which it normally lives.

flashcards.front: Name the three types of adaptation.
What is a structural adaptation? Give an example.
flashcards.back: A feature of body structure, for example thick fur, blubber or spines.

flashcards.front: What is a behavioural adaptation? Give an example.
flashcards.back: The way an organism behaves, for example migration, hibernation or being nocturnal.

flashcards.front: What is a functional adaptation? Give an example.
flashcards.back: An internal process such as metabolism or reproduction, for example producing concentrated urine.
An organism that lives in very extreme conditions: high temperature, high pressure or high salt concentration.

flashcards.front: Give an example of an extremophile.
flashcards.back: Bacteria living in deep sea vents.

flashcards.front: Why do Arctic animals have small ears?
flashcards.back: Smaller surface area to volume ratio, so less heat is lost.

flashcards.front: Why do desert foxes have large ears?
flashcards.back: Larger surface area to lose heat; ears have many blood vessels near the surface.

flashcards.front: How do cactus spines help it survive?
flashcards.back: They are reduced leaves, so less surface area for water loss; they also deter animals.

flashcards.front: Why are many desert animals nocturnal?
flashcards.back: It is cooler at night, so they lose less water and avoid overheating.

flashcards.front: Why do extremophile enzymes not denature at high temperatures?
flashcards.back: Their shape is adapted to stay stable at those temperatures.

flashcards.front: Name two adaptations of shade plants.
flashcards.back: Large broad leaves and lots of chlorophyll, to absorb as much light as possible.

questions.question: Which of these is a behavioural adaptation?
options: Thick fur
Migration to a warmer country in winter
Producing concentrated urine
Spines instead of leaves
markScheme: 1 mark: migration to a warmer country in winter
questions.explanation: Migration is something the animal does, so it is behavioural. Thick fur and spines are structural, and concentrated urine is functional.

questions.question: What is an extremophile?
options: An organism that only lives in rainforests
An organism that eats only one type of food
An organism that lives in very extreme conditions such as high temperature, pressure or salt concentration
An organism that has no adaptations
markScheme: 1 mark: an organism that lives in very extreme conditions
questions.explanation: Extremophiles survive conditions that would kill most organisms, such as boiling-hot vents or very salty lakes.

questions.question: Which of these is an extremophile?
options: Bacteria living in deep sea vents
Polar bears
Camels
Cacti
markScheme: 1 mark: bacteria living in deep sea vents
questions.explanation: Polar bears, camels and cacti are well adapted to harsh habitats, but deep sea vent bacteria live at extreme temperature and pressure, so they are the extremophile example.

questions.question: A polar bear has a thick layer of fat called blubber. What type of adaptation is this?
options: Behavioural
Functional
Reproductive
Structural
markScheme: 1 mark: structural
questions.explanation: Blubber is a physical feature of the body, so it is a structural adaptation that insulates the bear.

questions.question: A kangaroo rat lives in the desert and produces very concentrated urine. How does this help it survive?
options: It helps it lose heat
It conserves water
It makes it taste bad to predators
It helps it digest seeds
markScheme: 1 mark: it conserves water
questions.explanation: Concentrated urine means less water is lost in excretion: a functional adaptation for a dry habitat.

questions.question: Why do many woodland floor plants have large, broad leaves?
options: To reduce water loss
To store water
To absorb as much of the limited light as possible
To deter herbivores
markScheme: 1 mark: to absorb as much of the limited light as possible
questions.explanation: Light intensity is low under trees, so a large leaf area captures more light for photosynthesis. Large leaves actually increase water loss, which is less of a problem in moist shady woodland.

questions.question: Which feature would help an animal reduce heat loss in a cold climate?
options: A large surface area to volume ratio
Large thin ears
Thin fur
A small surface area to volume ratio
markScheme: 1 mark: a small surface area to volume ratio
questions.explanation: A small surface area compared with volume means less surface for heat to escape from. Large ears and thin fur increase heat loss, which suits hot climates.

questions.question:
A scientist grew bacteria from a deep sea vent at different temperatures.
Table 1 shows the results.
Which is the best explanation for the results?
options: Their enzymes are denatured at 30 °C
Their enzymes have an optimum temperature close to 90 °C, so reactions are slow at 30 °C
They need light to grow at 30 °C
They cannot respire when it is cool because oxygen is absent
markScheme: 1 mark: their enzymes have an optimum temperature close to 90 °C, so reactions are slow at 30 °C
questions.explanation: Enzymes are denatured by high, not low, temperatures. Extremophile enzymes are adapted to work best at high temperatures, so at 30 °C their reactions are too slow for growth.

questions.question: A hedgehog hibernates in winter and its metabolic rate falls greatly. Which statement correctly classifies these adaptations?
options: Hibernating is behavioural; the lower metabolic rate is functional
Both are structural
Hibernating is functional; the lower metabolic rate is behavioural
Both are behavioural
markScheme: 1 mark: hibernating is behavioural; the lower metabolic rate is functional
questions.explanation: Going into hibernation is a behaviour. The change in metabolism is a process inside the body, so it is functional. Neither is a body structure.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the temperature at the surface of a desert and inside a burrow 1 m below the surface.
Why do many desert animals spend the day in burrows and come out at night?
options: It is cooler at night so they lose less water
There is more light at night
Predators are only active during the day
They need less oxygen at night
markScheme: 1 mark: it is cooler at night so they lose less water
questions.explanation: Table 1 shows the burrow is much cooler than the surface during the day, and the surface is cool at night. Being nocturnal is a behavioural adaptation that avoids the heat of the day, reducing water loss by sweating or panting.

questions.question: What is meant by the term adaptation?
acceptedAnswers: enables an organism to survive in its environment
conditions in which it normally lives
markScheme: 1 mark: a feature that enables an organism to survive in the conditions in which it normally lives
questions.explanation: The key idea is a feature that helps survival in the organism's usual conditions.

questions.question: Give two adaptations of a polar bear that help it survive in the Arctic.
acceptedAnswers: small surface area to volume ratio
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two from: thick fur; layer of blubber (fat); white fur for camouflage; small ears; large body with small SA:V ratio; large feet or fur on soles for grip
questions.explanation: Most polar bear adaptations either reduce heat loss or help with hunting on snow and ice.

questions.question: Name the three types of adaptation.
markScheme: 1 mark: structural
1 mark: behavioural
1 mark: functional
questions.explanation: Structural adaptations are body features, behavioural are actions and functional are internal processes.

questions.question: Explain how a thick waxy cuticle helps a desert plant survive.
markScheme: 1 mark: the cuticle is waterproof / reduces evaporation from the surface
1 mark: so the plant conserves water in a habitat where water is scarce
questions.explanation: Always give the feature and its benefit linked to the habitat: water is scarce, so preventing water loss helps survival.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows the heads of two species of fox.
The fennec fox lives in the Sahara desert. Its very large ears contain many blood vessels.
Explain how the large ears help the fennec fox to survive in the desert.

figure.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 232" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="sans-serif"><path d="M72 118L48 22L102 108Z" fill="#fde68a" fill-opacity="0.5" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><path d="M148 118L172 22L118 108Z" fill="#fde68a" fill-opacity="0.5" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><path d="M68 118Q110 100 152 118L118 178Q110 186 102 178Z" fill="#fde68a" fill-opacity="0.5" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><circle cx="96" cy="132" r="3" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="124" cy="132" r="3" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="110" cy="176" r="4" fill="currentColor"/><text x="110" y="206" font-size="12" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle">Fennec fox</text><text x="110" y="222" font-size="12" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle">hot desert</text><path d="M254 120L256 92L274 110Z" fill="#e5e7eb" fill-opacity="0.5" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><path d="M326 120L324 92L306 110Z" fill="#e5e7eb" fill-opacity="0.5" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><path d="M248 118Q290 100 332 118L298 178Q290 186 282 178Z" fill="#e5e7eb" fill-opacity="0.5" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><circle cx="276" cy="132" r="3" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="304" cy="132" r="3" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="290" cy="176" r="4" fill="currentColor"/><text x="290" y="206" font-size="12" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle">Arctic fox</text><text x="290" y="222" font-size="12" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle">cold tundra</text></svg>

markScheme: 1 mark: large ears give a large surface area
1 mark: so more heat is transferred from the blood to the surroundings, helping the fox keep cool
questions.explanation: Large ears increase the surface area for heat loss. (They also help it hear prey underground, which is credit-worthy as an extra.)

questions.question: Explain how adaptations such as the white fur of the Arctic hare arise in a population over time.
markScheme: 1 mark: there is variation in fur colour in the population (caused by mutations)
1 mark: hares with whiter fur are better camouflaged, so more likely to survive predators and reproduce
1 mark: they pass on the alleles for white fur, so over many generations the feature becomes common
questions.explanation: Adaptations are the result of natural selection. Individuals do not change their fur because they need to; better-adapted individuals survive and breed more.

questions.question: Suggest why the enzymes of bacteria from a deep sea vent are useful in industry.
markScheme: 1 mark: they do not denature at high temperatures
1 mark: so industrial processes can be run hot, giving faster reactions (for example in DNA copying)
questions.explanation: Extremophile enzymes are adapted to remain active at very high temperatures, which normal enzymes cannot tolerate.

questions.question:
Classify each adaptation as structural, behavioural or functional:
(a) a snake basking in the sun in the morning
(b) a cactus storing water in its stem
markScheme: 1 mark: (a) behavioural
1 mark: (b) structural
questions.explanation: Basking is an action (behaviour). A swollen water-storing stem is a body feature (structural).

questions.question:
A student made a model of an animal.
Table 1 shows measurements of the model.
Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of the model.
questions.explanation: Surface area ÷ volume = 24 ÷ 8 = 3. This is a cube of side 2 cm.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows a cube-shaped model of an animal.
Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of the model.

figure.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 200" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="sans-serif"><path d="M60 70h90v90h-90Z" fill="#93c5fd" fill-opacity="0.5" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><path d="M60 70l40.5 -40.5h90l-40.5 40.5Z" fill="#93c5fd" fill-opacity="0.3" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><path d="M150 70l40.5 -40.5v90l-40.5 40.5Z" fill="#93c5fd" fill-opacity="0.7" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="105" y="178" font-size="12" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle"></text><text x="105" y="182" font-size="12" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle">4 cm</text><text x="205" y="125" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">4 cm</text><text x="74" y="46" font-size="12" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="end">4 cm</text></svg>

markScheme: 1 mark: surface area = 6 × 4 × 4 = 96 cm² and volume = 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 cm³
questions.explanation: A cube has 6 faces. 96 ÷ 64 = 1.5. Compare with a 1 cm cube (6 : 1): bigger animals have smaller ratios and lose heat more slowly.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows two cube-shaped models, A and B, that represent animals.
How many times larger is the surface area to volume ratio of model A than that of model B?

figure.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 230" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="sans-serif"><path d="M40 150h30v30h-30Z" fill="#93c5fd" fill-opacity="0.5" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><path d="M40 150l13.5 -13.5h30l-13.5 13.5Z" fill="#93c5fd" fill-opacity="0.3" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><path d="M70 150l13.5 -13.5v30l-13.5 13.5Z" fill="#93c5fd" fill-opacity="0.7" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="55" y="198" font-size="12" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle">A: sides 2 cm</text><path d="M200 100h90v90h-90Z" fill="#93c5fd" fill-opacity="0.5" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><path d="M200 100l40.5 -40.5h90l-40.5 40.5Z" fill="#93c5fd" fill-opacity="0.3" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><path d="M290 100l40.5 -40.5v90l-40.5 40.5Z" fill="#93c5fd" fill-opacity="0.7" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="245" y="208" font-size="12" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle">B: sides 6 cm</text></svg>

markScheme: 1 mark: 3 ÷ 1 = 3 times larger
questions.explanation: A: surface area 6 × 2² = 24 cm², volume 2³ = 8 cm³, ratio 3. B: 6 × 6² = 216 cm², 6³ = 216 cm³, ratio 1. So A's ratio is 3 times B's. Smaller animals lose heat faster, which is why Arctic mammals tend to be large.

questions.question:
A camel can lose up to 25% of its body mass as water without harm.
Calculate the mass of water a 600 kg camel could lose without harm.
markScheme: 1 mark: 150 kg
questions.explanation: 25% of 600 kg = 0.25 × 600 = 150 kg. Tolerating great water loss is a functional adaptation to desert life.

questions.question: Explain why cactus spines reduce water loss compared with broad leaves.
markScheme: 1 mark: spines have a much smaller surface area (and few or no stomata)
1 mark: so less water evaporates / less transpiration
questions.explanation: Water is lost mainly from leaf surfaces through stomata. Reducing leaves to spines massively cuts this surface.

questions.question: Some desert plants open their stomata only at night. Which type of adaptation is this, and what is its main benefit?
options: Structural: it increases light absorption
Behavioural: it helps the plant avoid predators
Functional: it reduces water loss because it is cooler at night
Functional: it increases photosynthesis in the day
markScheme: 1 mark: functional: it reduces water loss because it is cooler at night
questions.explanation: Opening stomata at night is a change in the plant's processes (functional). Cooler night air means less evaporation through the stomata.

questions.question: Give one extreme condition in which extremophiles can live.
markScheme: 1 mark: high temperature or high pressure or high salt concentration
questions.explanation: These are the three extreme conditions named in the AQA specification.

questions.question: A camel lives in hot, dry deserts. Describe and explain how the camel is adapted to survive. Use at least two different types of adaptation.
markScheme: Indicative content: structural: hump stores fat (energy) so little insulating fat elsewhere, easier heat loss; thin fur on most of body; long legs keep body away from hot sand; wide feet spread weight on sand; long eyelashes and closable nostrils keep sand out. Functional: produces little, concentrated urine and dry faeces to conserve water; can tolerate large water loss and body temperature changes; can drink large volumes quickly. Behavioural: rests in the shade or faces the sun to reduce surface exposed; sits with legs tucked.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): describes at least three adaptations, from at least two types, each with a correct explanation linked to heat or water.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): lists adaptations with little or no explanation, or one type only.
questions.explanation: Each adaptation needs a reason linked to the desert conditions. Using two types (for example structural and functional) shows full understanding.

questions.question:
The Arctic fox lives in the tundra, where winter temperatures fall to −40 °C. In summer the fox's fur is brown-grey; in winter it is thick and white. The fox has small ears, short legs and a compact body. In winter it curls up with its tail over its face.
Use this information and your own knowledge to explain how the Arctic fox is adapted to survive.
markScheme: Indicative content: thick winter fur traps air, an insulator, reducing heat loss (structural); small ears, short legs and compact body give a small surface area to volume ratio so less heat is lost (structural); white fur in winter camouflages it against snow, so it can approach prey and hide from predators; brown-grey summer fur camouflages it against rocks and plants; curling up with tail over face reduces the exposed surface area, reducing heat loss (behavioural); changing fur colour and thickness with the season is controlled by body processes (functional); together these let the fox maintain body temperature so enzymes work and it can hunt to obtain food.

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): explains at least four adaptations using correct scientific ideas (insulation, surface area to volume ratio, camouflage), including both structural and behavioural, with clear links to survival.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): explains two or three adaptations with some correct reasoning.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): identifies adaptations with little explanation.
questions.explanation: Use every clue in the stem and add a scientific reason to each. Naming the adaptation types and linking to survival (heat balance, hunting, avoiding predators) gives the highest level.

questions.question: Describe what extremophiles are and explain how bacteria living near deep sea vents are adapted to their environment.
markScheme: Indicative content: extremophiles live in extreme environments; high temperature, high pressure or high salt concentration; deep sea vents release very hot water (can be above 100 °C) at great depth and very high pressure; vent bacteria have enzymes that do not denature at high temperatures; their enzymes have high optimum temperatures; their cell structures (membranes, proteins) are stable at high pressure; there is no light, so they do not depend on photosynthesis.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): accurate definition and clear explanation of at least two adaptations to the vent conditions.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple definition or simple statement that they survive heat or pressure.
questions.explanation: The key adaptation is enzymes that remain active at high temperature. Mention both temperature and pressure for full credit.
